bib.title: Linear Model Selection and Regularization (Chapter 6, An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python)

question: How can the linear model be improved over plain least squares through subset selection, shrinkage and dimension reduction, and what changes when p is large relative to n?
contributions: Subset selection (best subset, forward, backward, hybrid) with Cp, AIC, BIC, adjusted R2 and CV for choosing size
Ridge regression and the lasso with geometric, soft-thresholding and Bayesian interpretations, lambda chosen by CV
Dimension reduction by PCR and PLS
High-dimensional pitfalls and a Python lab on Hitters with sklearn and ISLP

limits: Authors concede Cp, AIC, BIC justifications are asymptotic and beyond the book's scope; adjusted R2 is less well motivated in theory.
Simulation figures (6.5, 6.8, 6.9, 6.18, 6.19, 6.24) are illustrative; no seeds or repetition counts are given in the text.
The 5-fold CV standard error in the lab is crude because training sets overlap (footnote 9).
The lab prints a convergence-warning note for ridge via ElasticNet that the authors expect to disappear as the package matures (dated).
practices: Do not pick model size by training RSS or R2: they always improve with more variables; use Cp/AIC/BIC/adjusted R2, a validation set or CV (6.1.1, 6.1.3, p.231, 236).
Prefer CV over Cp/AIC/BIC now that compute is cheap; it needs no sigma2 estimate or degrees-of-freedom count (p.239).
When CV curve is flat, apply the one-standard-error rule: smallest model within one SE of the minimum (p.240).
With CV and subset selection, redo the whole selection inside each training fold; selecting on the full data biases the CV error (p.239, 271).
Standardise predictors before ridge, lasso, PCR and PLS, because the fit is not scale equivariant (p.242, 260, 262).
Use the lasso when few predictors matter and ridge when many have similar size, and decide between them by CV since the truth is unknown (p.248).
Choose lambda by CV on a grid then refit on all data; to estimate the tuned model's test error nest the CV inside an outer train/test split (p.252, 278).
Choose the number of PCR or PLS components M by CV (p.260, 262).
For p > n, use forward stepwise (backward needs n > p), ridge, lasso or PCR, and report test-set or CV error only (p.234-235, 265-267).
Do not interpret a selected variable set in high dimensions as the unique predictive set; validate on independent data (p.266-267).
Use sklearn Pipeline with StandardScaler plus the estimator inside GridSearchCV so scaling is refit per fold (p.275-277).

terms.definition: Fit a least squares regression for each possible combination of the p predictors and pick the best
Begins with no predictors and adds predictors one at a time, the one giving greatest additional improvement to the fit
Begins with the full least squares model and iteratively removes the least useful predictor; needs n > p
Cp = (RSS + 2 d sigma2-hat)/n, an estimate of test MSE; AIC is proportional for least squares
BIC = (RSS + log(n) d sigma2-hat)/n up to constants; heavier penalty than Cp when n > 7
Select the smallest model for which estimated test error is within one SE of the lowest point on the curve
Minimise RSS + lambda * sum of beta_j^2 (l2 penalty); shrinks but never zeroes coefficients
Minimise RSS + lambda * sum |beta_j| (l1 penalty); yields sparse models
Lasso shrinks each coefficient by a constant lambda/2 and sets those with |y_j| <= lambda/2 to zero (orthonormal case)
Construct first M principal components and use them as predictors in least squares; unsupervised directions
Supervised dimension reduction: first direction weights each standardised predictor by its simple regression coefficient on Y
Adding noise features not associated with the response raises test error, because they increase overfitting risk with no upside
Multiplying X_j by c scales the least squares coefficient by 1/c so X_j beta_j is unchanged; ridge lacks this

code.snippet:
def nCp(sigma2, estimator, X, Y):
    "Negative Cp statistic"
    n, p = X.shape
    Yhat = estimator.predict(X)
    RSS = np.sum((Y - Yhat)**2)
    return -(RSS + 2 * p * sigma2) / n

Xs = X - X.mean(0)[None,:]
X_scale = X.std(0)
Xs = Xs / X_scale[None,:]
lambdas = 10**np.linspace(8, -2, 100) / Y.std()
soln_array = skl.ElasticNet.path(Xs, Y, l1_ratio=0., alphas=lambdas)[1]

ridgeCV = skl.ElasticNetCV(alphas=lambdas, l1_ratio=0, cv=kfold)
pipeCV = Pipeline(steps=[('scaler', scaler), ('ridge', ridgeCV)])
pipeCV.fit(X, Y)

outer_valid = skm.ShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.25, random_state=1)
inner_cv = skm.KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=2)
ridgeCV = skl.ElasticNetCV(alphas=lambdas, l1_ratio=0, cv=inner_cv)
pipeCV = Pipeline(steps=[('scaler', scaler), ('ridge', ridgeCV)])
results = skm.cross_validate(pipeCV, X, Y, cv=outer_valid, scoring='neg_mean_squared_error')

lassoCV = skl.ElasticNetCV(n_alphas=100, l1_ratio=1, cv=kfold)
pipeCV = Pipeline(steps=[('scaler', scaler), ('lasso', lassoCV)])
